questions.question: What is the key limitation of a Sass variable (`$radius`) compared to a CSS custom property (`var(--radius)`)?
options: Sass variables are slower to parse in the browser
Sass variables are compiled away at build time and cannot be read or changed by JavaScript at runtime, unlike custom properties
Sass variables cannot hold color values
There is no real difference between them
questions.explanation: Sass compiles to plain CSS before it ever reaches the browser, so $radius simply becomes a literal value — there's no live variable left for JS to interact with, unlike a custom property.

questions.question: What does Autoprefixer actually do?
options: It reads a browserslist config and adds exactly the vendor prefixes still needed for your targeted browsers
It converts Sass to plain CSS
It adds all possible vendor prefixes to every property, regardless of target browsers
questions.explanation: Autoprefixer is a PostCSS plugin that targets prefixes based on real browser support data for the browsers you've configured, not a blanket catch-all.

questions.question: What best describes PostCSS itself?
options: A CSS preprocessor language like Sass
A tool that parses CSS into an AST and runs a pipeline of plugins over it — Autoprefixer being the most common one
questions.explanation: PostCSS itself defines no new syntax; its plugins (Autoprefixer, and others) are what actually transform the CSS.

questions.question: According to the lesson, where do Sass mixins still earn their place in a modern project that already uses Tailwind?
options: Nowhere — Sass should never be used alongside Tailwind
For genuinely complex, repeated patterns that would be verbose to express as utility classes
Sass and Tailwind cannot be used in the same project
questions.explanation: The two solve different problems — utility classes handle most day-to-day styling, while a mixin can still be the cleaner choice for a complex, reused rule set.
